Liquid Inference is an LLM inference marketplace from Architect where providers bid to serve each prompt. The buyer pays the lowest offer that meets its rules. For developers, it is quite simple message: swap a base URL, […] The post Architect Launches Liquid Inference, a Real-Time Auction for LLM Inference appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Architect Financial Technologies has launched Liquid Inference , an LLM router that runs a live auction for every request. Liquid Inference is an LLM inference marketplace from Architect where providers bid to serve each prompt. The buyer pays the lowest offer that meets its rules. For developers, it is quite simple message: swap a base URL, keep your code, and let providers compete on price. What is Liquid Inference? Liquid Inference is an exchange-style router for LLM inference. According to Architect , providers post offers to serve specific models. Each request is auctioned across every provider quoting the named model. The lowest-priced offer that meets the buyer’s rules wins. The product comes from a trading firm, not an AI lab. Architect runs the AX perpetual futures exchange . In May 2026 it acquired a US Designated Contract Market to list GPU compute futures, pending regulatory review. The team used its experience building financial exchanges to create two-sided price discovery for inference. How does the inference auction work? The flow has 4 steps: Request: A client sends a standard OpenAI or Anthropic API call. Rules: The buyer’s constraints filter eligible offers. Auction: Providers quoting that model compete. The lowest qualifying offer wins. Receipt: The max price is locked before generation. Billing covers metered usage only. Drop-in compatibility with agentic coding tools. The post lists Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Pi and Cline. Free email signup. The first 500 users get $20 of free inference, per Harrison. Providers onboard through the Liquid Inference app. Harrison says new providers are verified “in minutes, not weeks.” All prompts use the OpenAI API standard. A REST and WebSocket API registers models and quotes. Providers can update quotes based on their own costs. That lets them sell spare GPU capacity only when they want. PivotOPD on-policy distillation trains an agent to avoid its most damaging early mistake, and to recover when it happens anyway. Against 13 baselines, it posts the best average on ALFWorld, WebShop and Search-based QA for Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B students. The takeaway: recovery is learnable, and standard OPD rarely teaches it. TL;DR Size: A training method, not a model. Tested on Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B students, plus a Nemotron-3.5-SFT student on SWE-Bench Verified. Runs on: Trained on NVIDIA H100 nodes. Adds 0 inference cost, so the trained agent runs wherever its base model runs. Performance: First on all 8 per-benchmark averages against 13 baselines, across 3 seeds. Best: Recovers from 72.7% of replayed pivotal mistakes, vs 20.3% for standard OPD. Worst: 55.9% on ALFWorld “Look” tasks with the 1.7B student, vs 83.9% for SOD. Bottom line: Best: teaches recovery that outcome-only RL cannot reach. Worst: depends on replayable environments and a teacher whose pivots match the oracle in 77.8% of failed rollouts. What is a pivotal mistake in a multi-turn agent? A pivotal mistake is an action that lengthens the shortest remaining path to finishing a task, or makes it unsolvable. ALFWorld’s symbolic oracle measures this at every turn. Across Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3-235B-A22B, 59% of failed rollouts (155 of 262) contained one. The first pivotal turn arrived early, at a median of turn 8 to 12 out of 30. The agents then wasted 18 to 21 more turns without recovering. In replays of Qwen3-8B failures, correcting the pivotal turn raised success from 8% to 59%. Leaving the mistake in place and forcing the right action for the next 2 turns still reached 58%. For developers, the agent is […] The post Google Cloud Launches Gemini Agent, One Universal Agent for Enterprise Work appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Google Cloud has introduced the Google Cloud Gemini agent , a single agent for enterprise work. The Gemini agent is a cloud-hosted agent from Google Cloud that answers questions, does knowledge work, creates media, and writes and runs code. It does all of this from 1 prompt box and 1 API. For developers, the agent is the product and the model is a routing decision. TL;DR Runs on: Google Cloud (AI Hypercomputer). Reached from web, mobile, desktop, CLI, Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, or headless. Best: Bloomberg Media lifted SQL query accuracy by 63% by grounding data agents in Knowledge Catalog. Bottom line: Best: 1 governed agent with cloud memory, sub-agents and hard spend caps. Worst: buyers must evaluate it on customer anecdotes, not reproducible numbers. What is the Google Cloud Gemini agent? It is a delegation layer, not a chatbot. You give it objectives, not instructions. It plans the work, picks skills and tools, connects to company systems, and returns finished output. Google lists 6 architectural principles: Unified agent: chat, autonomous objectives and code generation share 1 interface. Omnipresent access: any device or channel, plus embedding in third-party apps. Persistent execution: it runs in the cloud with 1 set of memories and 1 personalization graph. Jobs lasting hours or days keep running after you close the laptop. Multi-agent orchestration: it creates temporary sub-agents, each with its own identity, and runs parallel or sequential steps. Deeply contextual: it learns your tools, data and work history over time. Model choice flexibility: each job runs on the best-fit model. Today at Google Cloud’s Gemini at Work event, we announced Gemini, a new single universal agent for work that has all of your business context and can be used for everything from knowledge work to answering questions, and content creation to coding, all from a single prompt box.… pic.twitter.com/2Z1PZg74Ui — Thomas Kurian (@ThomasOrTK) October 8, 2026 How does the Gemini agent remember and reason? It keeps 4 kinds of memory. Session memory covers the current task, even across days. Semantic memory is a structured knowledge base it builds from documents and people. Procedural memory stores how jobs get done, including skills it writes for itself. Episodic memory records everything it has done before. Skills are modular prompts stored in a shared company registry. Tools come from an enterprise tools registry. Connectors cover Slack, Jira, Salesforce, ServiceNow, BigQuery, Snowflake, desktop files and any Model Context Protocol server. Which models does it use? Today it orchestrates across Google’s Gemini models and Claude models from Anthropic , with other private and open models planned. Google’s own lineup is Argon for frontier reasoning, Flash for speed and volume, Omni for generative media, and Gemma for open-weights edge work. What are coworker agents? A coworker agent is a persistent teammate with a defined role. In Workspace it receives its own account: email address, calendar, Drive and a directory entry. Colleagues @mention it in Chat or Docs, and its edits appear under its own name in version history. It sees only what is shared with it. The agent also works inline across Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Chat and Calendar, and offers 1-click delegation of tasks it spots. What does it add for data teams? Data and ML engineers describe outcomes in plain language. The agent then writes PySpark code, provides notebooks, trains models and fixes pipeline issues. Business users get saved BigQuery reports that rerun without token costs. Three services ground the answers. Knowledge Catalog maps business definitions once for every agent. Smart Storage enriches unstructured objects in place; Google says 90% of enterprise data is unstructured. Borderless Lakehouse queries Amazon S3 and Azure Data Lake with no variable egress fees. How is the agent governed? Google frames governance as 4 questions: who, what it may do, what it did, and what it must never touch. Identity: each agent gets a cryptographically attested identity with least-privilege permissions. Authorization: role-based access, mapped to external systems through standards such as OAuth. Auditing: every action is logged to the agent, not a person. Policy: agents run in an Agent Sandbox. All traffic passes through Agent Gateway, an AI network firewall that applies 1 policy to every agent. How does Google control cost? Three levers: multi-model orchestration, Smart Routing that triages workloads to the cheapest capable model, and real-time spend caps. Teams set a hard project limit in the Cloud Billing Console. When it triggers, that project’s agent pauses until someone resumes it. Underneath, Google team states its TPU 8i system delivers 80% better price-performance than the prior generation. How does it compare? And whether you choose to work primarily from home or collaborate in-person from one of our offices in Columbus, Austin, the Bay Area, or New York City, you’ll have the support to work in the way that works best for you.</p> <p>If you’re energized by tackling meaningful problems, excited to innovate with purpose, and motivated by work that truly matters, we’d love to hear from you.</p></div><div class="sc-kkmypM jItuJQ MuiStack-root">&nbsp;</div> <p><strong>The Role</strong></p> <p>As an Applied Scientist Intern, you will become a specialist in our models, products, business and/or codebase. You will receive mentorship from experienced ML practitioners and collaborate closely with the team to improve our products and models.</p> <p><strong>How you’ll make an impact</strong></p> <ul> <li>Research machine learning and statistical approaches to discover improvements to the predictive performance and/or business value of a model.</li> <li>Design, implement, and evaluate model, product, or technical enhancements using rigorous experimentation and validation methods.</li> <li>Translate research findings into clear recommendations, documented methodologies, and production-ready solutions.</li> <li>Work with your mentor to align stakeholders, and drive next steps.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Minimum Qualifications&nbsp;</strong></p> <ul> <li>Bachelor. To this end, over the course of the internship, you will meet to collaborate once or twice, for 2-4 consecutive days at a time.</p> <p><strong>What you'll love</strong></p> <p>At Upstart, our intern benefits are designed to support your health, financial well-being, and everyday needs while you’re here. For developers, the agent is […] The post Google Cloud Launches Gemini Agent, One Universal Agent for Enterprise Work appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Google Cloud has introduced the Google Cloud Gemini agent , a single agent for enterprise work. The Gemini agent is a cloud-hosted agent from Google Cloud that answers questions, does knowledge work, creates media, and writes and runs code. It does all of this from 1 prompt box and 1 API. For developers, the agent is the product and the model is a routing decision. TL;DR Runs on: Google Cloud (AI Hypercomputer). Reached from web, mobile, desktop, CLI, Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, or headless. Best: Bloomberg Media lifted SQL query accuracy by 63% by grounding data agents in Knowledge Catalog. Bottom line: Best: 1 governed agent with cloud memory, sub-agents and hard spend caps. Worst: buyers must evaluate it on customer anecdotes, not reproducible numbers. What is the Google Cloud Gemini agent? It is a delegation layer, not a chatbot. You give it objectives, not instructions. It plans the work, picks skills and tools, connects to company systems, and returns finished output. Google lists 6 architectural principles: Unified agent: chat, autonomous objectives and code generation share 1 interface. Omnipresent access: any device or channel, plus embedding in third-party apps. Persistent execution: it runs in the cloud with 1 set of memories and 1 personalization graph. Jobs lasting hours or days keep running after you close the laptop. Multi-agent orchestration: it creates temporary sub-agents, each with its own identity, and runs parallel or sequential steps. Deeply contextual: it learns your tools, data and work history over time. Model choice flexibility: each job runs on the best-fit model. Today at Google Cloud’s Gemini at Work event, we announced Gemini, a new single universal agent for work that has all of your business context and can be used for everything from knowledge work to answering questions, and content creation to coding, all from a single prompt box.… pic.twitter.com/2Z1PZg74Ui — Thomas Kurian (@ThomasOrTK) October 8, 2026 How does the Gemini agent remember and reason? It keeps 4 kinds of memory. Session memory covers the current task, even across days. Semantic memory is a structured knowledge base it builds from documents and people. Procedural memory stores how jobs get done, including skills it writes for itself. Episodic memory records everything it has done before. Skills are modular prompts stored in a shared company registry. Tools come from an enterprise tools registry. Connectors cover Slack, Jira, Salesforce, ServiceNow, BigQuery, Snowflake, desktop files and any Model Context Protocol server. Which models does it use? Today it orchestrates across Google’s Gemini models and Claude models from Anthropic , with other private and open models planned. Google’s own lineup is Argon for frontier reasoning, Flash for speed and volume, Omni for generative media, and Gemma for open-weights edge work. What are coworker agents? A coworker agent is a persistent teammate with a defined role. In Workspace it receives its own account: email address, calendar, Drive and a directory entry. Colleagues @mention it in Chat or Docs, and its edits appear under its own name in version history. It sees only what is shared with it. The agent also works inline across Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Chat and Calendar, and offers 1-click delegation of tasks it spots. What does it add for data teams? Data and ML engineers describe outcomes in plain language. The agent then writes PySpark code, provides notebooks, trains models and fixes pipeline issues. Business users get saved BigQuery reports that rerun without token costs. Three services ground the answers. Knowledge Catalog maps business definitions once for every agent. Smart Storage enriches unstructured objects in place; Google says 90% of enterprise data is unstructured. Borderless Lakehouse queries Amazon S3 and Azure Data Lake with no variable egress fees. How is the agent governed? Google frames governance as 4 questions: who, what it may do, what it did, and what it must never touch. Identity: each agent gets a cryptographically attested identity with least-privilege permissions. Authorization: role-based access, mapped to external systems through standards such as OAuth. Auditing: every action is logged to the agent, not a person. Policy: agents run in an Agent Sandbox. All traffic passes through Agent Gateway, an AI network firewall that applies 1 policy to every agent. How does Google control cost? Three levers: multi-model orchestration, Smart Routing that triages workloads to the cheapest capable model, and real-time spend caps. Teams set a hard project limit in the Cloud Billing Console. When it triggers, that project’s agent pauses until someone resumes it. Underneath, Google team states its TPU 8i system delivers 80% better price-performance than the prior generation. How does it compare? Routes jobs across Gemini and Claude models today. Coworker agents get their own Workspace identity. Hard per-project spend caps pause runaway agents. No benchmarks, price or GA date yet. Underdog tuned the compression to protect tool calling, the skill that turns a chat model into an agent. For developers, that means a 27B-class agent model that runs in stock llama.cpp . TL;DR Size: 27B dense parameters. 7.89 GB GGUF versus 54 GB for BF16. Runs on: stock llama.cpp and apps built on it, with full GPU offload. Optional 629 MB or 928 MB vision add-on. Performance: 96% average retention across 9 benchmarks versus full Qwen3.8-27B. Best: Parallel tool calls, 42 versus 35 for the full model (120% retention). Worst: AIME 2025, 79.2 versus 96.7 (about 82% retention). Bottom line: Best: beats the 54 GB original at tool calling in a sub-8 GB file. Worst: competition math and multi-step reasoning drop 12 to 18 points. What is Underdog Saluki 27B? Saluki 27B is a 2-bit, mixed-precision GGUF of Qwen3.8-27B built for local agents. It stacks 3 layers of work : The base is Qwen3.8-27B, a dense 27B model from the Qwen team. It has 64 layers, mixes Gated DeltaNet linear attention with gated attention, and supports 262,144 tokens natively . The second layer is ISTA-DASLab’s Qwen3.8-27B-GSQ-RCO-GGUF . GSQ learns accurate low-bit scalar grids per tensor. RCO assigns a quantization type to each tensor under a fixed size budget. ISTA’s smallest file, IQ2_XS, is 8.4 GB at 2.50 bits per weight. The third layer is Underdog’s own pass. It shrank the file to 7.89 GB and targeted tool calling. The file is named IQ2-mix and carries an imatrix tag. Underdog has not published the full recipe for this pass. How does Saluki perform on benchmarks? Underdog splits its results into 2 groups. The first group ran both models in the same harness : Underdog Bench: 120 tasks from BFCL v4 , frozen before testing. Thinking off, temperature 0. Saluki scores 88, the full model 84, and PrismML’s Bonsai 2 scores 70. Parallel tool calls: 100 BFCL v4 parallel tasks with the official checker. Saluki 42, full model 35. SWE-bench Verified: 50 issues. Saluki fixes 30, the full model 33. The second group compares Saluki with public full-size scores: Benchmark Saluki 27B Qwen3.8-27B (public) IFEval (prompt-loose) 93.5 91.5 IFBench (prompt-loose) 72.7 71.0 MBPP+ 78.0 83.9 MuSR 67.5 79.6 AIME 2025 (avg@4) 79.2 96.7 AIME 2026 (avg@4) 80.0 94.6 How does Saluki compare with other compact Qwen3.8-27B builds? The Gemini agent is a cloud-hosted agent from Google Cloud that answers questions, does knowledge work, creates media, and writes and runs code. It does all of this from 1 prompt box and 1 API. For developers, the agent is the product and the model is a routing decision. TL;DR Runs on: Google Cloud (AI Hypercomputer). Bottom line: Best: 1 governed agent with cloud memory, sub-agents and hard spend caps. Worst: buyers must evaluate it on customer anecdotes, not reproducible numbers. What is the Google Cloud Gemini agent? It is a delegation layer, not a chatbot. You give it objectives, not instructions. It plans the work, picks skills and tools, connects to company systems, and returns finished output. Google lists 6 architectural principles: Unified agent: chat, autonomous objectives and code generation share 1 interface. Omnipresent access: any device or channel, plus embedding in third-party apps. Persistent execution: it runs in the cloud with 1 set of memories and 1 personalization graph. Jobs lasting hours or days keep running after you close the laptop. Multi-agent orchestration: it creates temporary sub-agents, each with its own identity, and runs parallel or sequential steps. Deeply contextual: it learns your tools, data and work history over time. Model choice flexibility: each job runs on the best-fit model. oldContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Wed, 07 Oct 2026 19:36:03 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.9 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Exclusive: Gudea Lands $7M To Predict Which Online Narratives Will Go Viral https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/gudea-lands-funding-predict-viral-online-narratives/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 13:00:02 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94196 Gudea has raised $7 million in seed funding to help companies anticipate which online narratives will go viral and understand who is driving them, the startup tells Crunchbase News exclusively. Mudita Venture Partners and Silicon Road Ventures co-led the round, bringing the Minneapolis-based startup’s total funding to about $15 million since its 2023 inception, according to co-founder and CEO Keith Presley . The company says its revenue has grown 357% year over year. Its customers include major AI companies and businesses in telecommunications, entertainment and retail, although it declined to identify them, citing the sensitive nature of its work. Gudea’s premise is that tracking mentions and hashtags tells companies only part of the story. The startup aims to map how information moves across people, groups and platforms, then predict how far a narrative will spread, when it will take off, and when it will fade. Presley describes Gudea as the “storm tracker for the internet.” “As a meteorologist uses patterns to predict the weather, we’re using patterns to predict information,” he said in an interview, adding that the startup covers over 600 social media platforms. From disrupting disinformation to tracking brands Gudea’s management team, from left: Matt Chase, Jonathan Sperber, James Thomin, Georgia Paul and Keith Presley. (Courtesy photo) The business grew out of the George Washington Initiative, a nonprofit that adapted tactics used by the intelligence community to disrupt online Al Qaeda and ISIS networks for domestic information campaigns. The team initially searched for existing software that could show how information traveled, but found social listening tools insufficient. James Thomin , Gudea’s CTO and one of its founders, began working on technology to map those pathways. When the team examined the backlash around Bud Light’s marketing campaign with actor Dylan Mulvaney, it reached a turning point. The campaign’s critics used the same information pathways that had carried COVID disinformation, noted Presley. The team realized “that these patterns were repeating, and that there was a much broader use case,” he recalled. The technology spun out into a company in 2023. Its initial commercial focus has been reputational risk management, which entails helping large businesses spot potentially consequential stories before they spread widely. “We don’t need to know what we’re looking for to find it, so we can find all of those good or bad narratives before you know what keywords you should be searching for,” Presley said. Who’s driving the conversation? One way Gudea operates is by assessing whether users or accounts exhibiting unusual behavior are driving online conversations. It also examines how narratives move from less visible online communities into more mainstream platforms. For example, the startup conducted an analysis of online claims linking Taylor Swift to Nazism around an album release. 1 Georgia Paul , Gudea’s director of client experience, told Crunchbase News that the analysis uncovered that the narrative was being manipulated. The company says its work has also involved cases of corporate espionage and stock market manipulation. More recently, it has been examining how conversations about data centers affect businesses in AI and energy. Its technology can also identify positive trends companies might capitalize on, according to Paul, in addition to reputational threats. Predicting what spreads next Gudea uses deep learning, including graph neural networks, to analyze behavior, and uses a large language model to summarize findings. “Those behavior patterns are like fingerprints, and so our AI then recognizes those fingerprints, pulls it out, and then we use an LLM to summarize,” Presley said. The company sells its software to businesses through offerings that include alerts, platform access and automatically delivered reports. The latter emerged from its work with senior teams that were unlikely to log into a platform themselves. Presley cited Blackbird , Cyabra and Alethea as competitors in narrative intelligence, while positioning Gudea’s predictions as its distinguishing feature. Gudea tells customers “how long till it goes viral, how many people will be impacted, and how long till it goes away,” he said. For Gudea, the broader aim remains connected to its nonprofit origins: making the mechanisms behind online information more visible. “People are making real-world decisions off of what they see online, and not all of that information is authentic,” Presley said. The startup plans to use its new capital to expand its team, develop new features and broaden its coverage across platforms, languages and regions. It currently has 39 customers and approximately 25 employees. Buddy Foster , investor at Mudita Venture Partners, notes that AI is changing how stories are spread on the internet. “Damage to a brand is now starting in the fringe parts of the internet and builds momentum before it ever reaches a headline. It’s a big problem,” he wrote via email. “Gudea has built a solution that has the potential to own the market and know more than just the headlines. They can really see what is coming before it’s a problem.” Most other tools on the market are “reactive and surface-layer,” in Foster’s view, whereas Gudea is more proactive. “Gudea models how information moves across the internet and hundreds of platforms, so it can spot a problem before anyone knows to search for it,” he added. “Since it looks at behavior instead of content, its ability to be proactive gets better even as the internet gets more clouded.” Related Crunchbase query: Global Venture Funding To AI Startups In 2026 Illustration: Dom Guzman Gudea conducted that research for press coverage rather than for Swift, who was not a client. ↩ ]]> https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/Money_Rocket.jpg Europe Posted Its Strongest Quarter In Q3 In 4 Years, As Its Venture Ecosystem Expands Beyond The UK https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/q3-2026-europe-strong-quarter-ai-uk-germany-france/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 11:00:56 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94198 In Q3, Europe posted its strongest venture funding quarter in four years, with AI companies driving those gains, Crunchbase data shows. European startup funding reached $25 billion last quarter, well above the $14 billion invested in Q3 2025 and up slightly from the $24 billion invested in Q2. Quarterly funding was up 77% year over year, per Crunchbase data. While the U.K. continued to lead startup funding totals last quarter, Germany and France both posted their strongest quarters since the boom years of 2021 and early 2022. Last quarter’s funding totals were boosted heavily by a $3.5 billion investment in Paris-based Mistral , the largest venture round ever for a Europe-based company. Per Crunchbase data, a majority of the most active venture investors in Q3 participated in more deals compared to the prior quarter. This includes many of the usual busiest dealmakers, like Andreessen Horowitz , Insight Partners and Sequoia Capital . The top lead venture investors also largely stepped up the pace this past quarter, even as the highest-spending among them appeared to put less capital to work. At seed stage, meanwhile, the typical top dealmakers largely held their ranks. For a more detailed look, below we chart and analyze the most active investor ranks across multiple metrics, including venture dealmakers, high spenders, lead backers and seed funders. Most active venture investors We’ll start with the most active investors in post-seed rounds. By this measure, Y Combinator topped the ranks with 45 deals. The famed accelerator typically ranks high because it participates in follow-on rounds for startups it incubates. Next on the list were Andreessen Horowitz, Insight Partners and Sequoia Capital. Overall, as charted below, at least 22 investors participated in 10 or more known venture rounds this past quarter. Busiest lead investors Among lead investors in venture rounds, Insight, Andreessen and Khosla Ventures ranked highest with 18, 16 and 12 rounds, respectively. Another three investors — Valor Equity Partners , Sequoia and Atreides Management — had 10 lead deals each in Q3. Spendiest lead investors We also attempted to get a sense of which lead investors put the most capital work in Q3. To approximate this, our ranking looks at investors whose lead rounds had the highest aggregate value. 1 By this metric, Valor and Atreides tied for the No. 1 slot, with $7.7 billion in led or co-led deals for the quarter. The two had some overlap, with at least six rounds this past quarter listing both firms as lead investors. This included Crusoe ’s $3.9 billion Series F and Positron ’s $375 million Series C. Next in the ranking were Andreessen Horowitz and Nvidia , with $6.5 billion and $6.3 billion in led or co-led Q3 deals. Andreessen’s tally largely stemmed from a $2 billion round for Cognition and a $1.7 billion financing for Atoms . Nvidia’s standout deal was a $5 billion round for Safe Superintelligence . Seed investors Seed investors also kept busy in Q3. Among them, the busiest by far was Y Combinator, which participated in at least 221 known seed rounds this past quarter, per Crunchbase data. Antler also ranked high, with 31 reported seed rounds, followed by LvlUp Ventures and Rebel Fund with 24 and 23 reported deals, respectively. Overall, another busy, AI-driven quarter Overall, our active investor rankings paint the picture of another busy quarter for startup funding, with AI driving the bulk of dealmaking. Mostly, it’s familiar names topping our various rankings. However, we are seeing a few firms significantly scaling up their investments, with Atreides and Valor in particular stepping up their game of late. However, in most cases lead backers contribute a significant share to a financing, particularly if there are few investors or lead investors in that deal. ↩ ]]> https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/money-increasing.jpg Why Customer Workflows Are Becoming The Moat In The AI Era https://news.crunchbase.com/ma/customer-workflows-moat-ai-era-sagie/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 11:00:36 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94208 Imagine an insurance company testing two AI assistants. Both understand customer questions, respond naturally and perform well in demonstrations. Six months later, one handles policy renewals inside the insurer’s systems, follows approval rules and escalates exceptions to employees. The other remains a tool people occasionally open. A better model could arrive tomorrow, but replacing the first assistant would require changing how the company operates. That is where I believe an important AI moat is developing: inside customer workflows. Recent acquisitions and partnerships illustrate three implications for founders, investors and boards. Workflow access creates strategic value Schneider Electric ’s agreement to acquire PTC for approximately $22.6 billion in equity value gives it software used to design, manufacture and service physical products, placing it inside customer decisions throughout a product’s lifecycle. Meanwhile, the Synopsys – OpenAI partnership illustrates a similar logic: Combining frontier AI with established chip-design tools and expertise, supported by licensing and revenue sharing. My reading is that these transactions highlight the strategic value of owning the environment in which AI performs useful work. Companies already embedded in complex industries bring customer relationships, domain expertise and trusted processes that AI developers need to commercialize their technology. For founders, that suggests building a position inside a specific customer workflow. For established businesses, it creates an opportunity to turn existing workflow access into bargaining power. Completing recurring work builds defensibility ElevenLabs reported that its agents handle more than 15 million conversations weekly, including refunds, insurance renewals and healthcare bookings, alongside announcing an employee tender at a $22 billion valuation. The operational adoption is particularly relevant to the moat discussion. Once a product connects to internal systems, follows permissions, handles exceptions and reliably completes tasks, replacing it involves migration, testing, retraining and operational risk. This can strengthen retention and create opportunities to serve additional workflows. Integration alone offers limited protection, however. Customers need to depend on the product and measure the value it delivers. Investors should therefore examine how much recurring work flows through the platform, which processes rely on it, and what switching would actually require. Companies can acquire their way into workflows ServiceNow ’s acquisition of Moveworks combines an AI assistant and enterprise search technology with established workflow automation. At completion, Moveworks had 5.5 million employee users, with approximately 250 customers already using both companies’ technologies. The strategic opportunity is to connect employee requests directly to the systems and processes that resolve them across IT, HR and other functions. This creates a clear corp dev agenda: identify the customer workflows the company wants to enter, understand the barriers, and assess whether an acquisition or partnership can accelerate entry. An attractive target may bring technology, customer relationships, integrations and an established role in daily operations. Underdog Saluki 27B is a 2-bit GGUF of Qwen3.8-27B that fits in 7.89 GB. The full BF16 model needs 54 GB. Underdog tuned the compression to protect tool calling, the skill that turns a chat model into an agent. For developers, that means a 27B-class agent model that runs in stock llama.cpp . TL;DR Size: 27B dense parameters. 7.89 GB GGUF versus 54 GB for BF16. Runs on: stock llama.cpp and apps built on it, with full GPU offload. Optional 629 MB or 928 MB vision add-on. Performance: 96% average retention across 9 benchmarks versus full Qwen3.8-27B. Best: Parallel tool calls, 42 versus 35 for the full model (120% retention). Worst: AIME 2025, 79.2 versus 96.7 (about 82% retention). Bottom line: Best: beats the 54 GB original at tool calling in a sub-8 GB file. Worst: competition math and multi-step reasoning drop 12 to 18 points. What is Underdog Saluki 27B? Saluki 27B is a 2-bit, mixed-precision GGUF of Qwen3.8-27B built for local agents. It stacks 3 layers of work : The base is Qwen3.8-27B, a dense 27B model from the Qwen team. It has 64 layers, mixes Gated DeltaNet linear attention with gated attention, and supports 262,144 tokens natively . The second layer is ISTA-DASLab’s Qwen3.8-27B-GSQ-RCO-GGUF . GSQ learns accurate low-bit scalar grids per tensor. RCO assigns a quantization type to each tensor under a fixed size budget. ISTA’s smallest file, IQ2_XS, is 8.4 GB at 2.50 bits per weight. The third layer is Underdog’s own pass. It shrank the file to 7.89 GB and targeted tool calling. The file is named IQ2-mix and carries an imatrix tag. Underdog has not published the full recipe for this pass. How does Saluki perform on benchmarks? Underdog splits its results into 2 groups. The first group ran both models in the same harness : Underdog Bench: 120 tasks from BFCL v4 , frozen before testing. Thinking off, temperature 0. Saluki scores 88, the full model 84, and PrismML’s Bonsai 2 scores 70. Parallel tool calls: 100 BFCL v4 parallel tasks with the official checker. Saluki 42, full model 35. SWE-bench Verified: 50 issues. Saluki fixes 30, the full model 33. The second group compares Saluki with public full-size scores: Benchmark Saluki 27B Qwen3.8-27B (public) IFEval (prompt-loose) 93.5 91.5 IFBench (prompt-loose) 72.7 71.0 MBPP+ 78.0 83.9 MuSR 67.5 79.6 AIME 2025 (avg@4) 79.2 96.7 AIME 2026 (avg@4) 80.0 94.6 How does Saluki compare with other compact Qwen3.8-27B builds? It also posts stronger math, including 95.00 on AIME25. However, it needs PrismML’s llama.cpp fork, since stock llama.cpp rejects its packing formats. Saluki runs on stock llama.cpp. Each vendor uses its own harness, so cross-vendor scores are not directly comparable. Key Takeaways Saluki 27B fits Qwen3.8-27B into 7.89 GB, down from 54 GB. Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo is an […] The post Alibaba Qwen Releases Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo, an 8-Step 7B Image Model appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Alibaba’s Qwen team has released Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo , an accelerated checkpoint of its open-weight Qwen-Image-2.1 model. It generates and edits images in 8 denoising steps instead of the base model’s 40-step default . For developers, that means 5x fewer denoising steps on the same 7B architecture, plus a hosted API option. TL;DR Size: 7B parameters in the visual generator, paired with a Qwen3-VL 8B text encoder . Runs on: CUDA GPUs in BF16 via Diffusers. Qwen publishes no Turbo VRAM minimum. Unsloth estimates the base model runs on 11 GB VRAM with GGUF and 24 GB with INT8/FP8 . Performance: Same 2K output and editing feature set as Qwen-Image-2.1, at 8 steps instead of 40. Best: Base Qwen-Image-2.1 scores 60.28 on Qwen-Image-Bench, the top open-weight score Qwen reports. Bottom line (best): 8-step 2K generation and editing in one open checkpoint. Bottom line (worst): Research license only, so commercial self-hosting needs separate permission. What is Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo? Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo is an 8-step image generation and editing checkpoint from Alibaba’s Qwen team. It is built on Qwen-Image-2.1 . Turbo keeps the same 7B visual generation architecture. It loads directly with QwenImage21Pipeline in Diffusers. The checkpoint ships with its recommended 8-step sampling schedule saved inside. Generation uses CFG=1 by default. Prefix KV caching reuses the text and reference-image context across denoising steps. How does Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo work? The underlying architecture is a single-stream DiT with 32 layers and 7B parameters. It uses block-causal attention. Text tokens get a token-level causal mask, while images use a chunk-level bidirectional mask. Text encoder: Qwen3-VL 8B encodes both instructions and condition images. VAE: a 64-channel RGBA autoencoder with 16x spatial compression, which enables native transparency. Scheduler: Flow Matching with Euler discrete scheduling and dynamic shifting. The attention design is what makes prefix caching work. Input images and text are computed once at the first step. Every later step reuses that cache. With only 8 steps, the cached prefix covers most of the conditioning cost. What can it generate and edit? The Turbo model card showcase covers 8 categories. These include portraits, human poses, transparent images, typography and posters, and UI layouts. Editing examples include single-image transformation, multi-reference composition and 4-image interior composition. The base model supports up to 10 reference images and local edits via circles, painted annotations or masks. How do you run Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo? Setup requires Diffusers from source , along with transformers>=5.17.0 . The checkpoint needs Diffusers PR #14950 , which adds pipeline-configured sampling sigmas. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser import torch from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained( "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo", dtype=torch.bfloat16 ).to("cuda") image = pipe( prompt="A ceramic teapot on a wooden table, soft window light", width=2048, height=2048, use_kv_cache=True, ).images[0] For editing, pass image=input_image with an instruction prompt. Supported presets run from 2048×2048 square to 2752×1536 at 16:9. One thing to note here. Setting num_inference_steps alone does not override the saved schedule. Only an explicit sigmas argument does, and Qwen notes other schedules are untested. What does the API cost? Alibaba Cloud Model Studio now hosts both Turbo and Pro. qwen-image-2.1-turbo costs CNY 0.1 per image in most regions, with a 120 RPM limit. qwen-image-2.1-pro costs CNY 0.25 per image, with 20 RPM. Turbo is 2.5x cheaper per image and allows 6x the request rate. A better model could arrive tomorrow, but replacing the first assistant would require changing how the company operates. That is where I believe an important AI moat is developing: inside customer workflows. Recent acquisitions and partnerships illustrate three implications for founders, investors and boards. Workflow access creates strategic value Schneider Electric ’s agreement to acquire PTC for approximately $22.6 billion in equity value gives it software used to design, manufacture and service physical products, placing it inside customer decisions throughout a product’s lifecycle. Meanwhile, the Synopsys – OpenAI partnership illustrates a similar logic: Combining frontier AI with established chip-design tools and expertise, supported by licensing and revenue sharing. My reading is that these transactions highlight the strategic value of owning the environment in which AI performs useful work. Companies already embedded in complex industries bring customer relationships, domain expertise and trusted processes that AI developers need to commercialize their technology. For founders, that suggests building a position inside a specific customer workflow. For established businesses, it creates an opportunity to turn existing workflow access into bargaining power. Completing recurring work builds defensibility ElevenLabs reported that its agents handle more than 15 million conversations weekly, including refunds, insurance renewals and healthcare bookings, alongside announcing an employee tender at a $22 billion valuation. The operational adoption is particularly relevant to the moat discussion. Once a product connects to internal systems, follows permissions, handles exceptions and reliably completes tasks, replacing it involves migration, testing, retraining and operational risk. This can strengthen retention and create opportunities to serve additional workflows. Integration alone offers limited protection, however. Customers need to depend on the product and measure the value it delivers. Investors should therefore examine how much recurring work flows through the platform, which processes rely on it, and what switching would actually require. Companies can acquire their way into workflows ServiceNow ’s acquisition of Moveworks combines an AI assistant and enterprise search technology with established workflow automation. Check out T he Crunchbase Megadeals Board . This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here . As the AI startup boom progresses, investors appear to be leaving few niches unfunded. That was apparent in this week’s lineup of large funding rounds, which featured AI infrastructure providers, a foundational model developer, a content protection platform for the AI age, and other AI-focused startups among the top investment recipients. The biggest investment, $2 billion, went to Axiom Solutions International , a spinout focused on cloud and power infrastructure that is hoping to benefit from the AI buildout. Other large rounds went to TypeSafe AI , developer of a fast-growing new model, and Oratomic , a quantum computing startup. 1. Axiom Solutions International , $2B, cloud and power infrastructure: Axiom Solutions International, a private cloud and power infrastructure company spun out of manufacturing services provider Flex , secured $2 billion in new financing. General Catalyst and Koch Equity provided the strategic investment by purchasing shares of Austin-based Axiom from Flex at an initial enterprise value of $37.5 billion. Flex says it plans to separate Axiom into an independent publicly traded company early next year. 2. TypeSafe AI , $870M, foundational AI: TypeSafe AI, developer of Jev, a recently launched AI model with a large and growing early following, raised $870 million in new funding with Andreessen Horowitz as the largest investor, according to a Bloomberg report . Sequoia Capital also participated in the round, which reportedly set a $7.5 billion valuation for San Francisco-based TypeSafe. 3. Oratomic , $475M, quantum computing: Pasadena, California-based Oratomic, a startup working on fault-tolerant quantum computers, raised $475 million in fresh funding led by Arch Venture Partners , Spark Capital , Khosla Ventures , Index Ventures , General Catalyst and Bezos Expeditions . The company previously raised $300 million in a July financing. 4. SignSplit , $400M, data and content protection: SignSplit, a provider of tools for protecting, licensing and contributing real-world human data and other forms of human contribution, emerged from stealth with $400 million in seed funding. W Group backed the round, setting a $1 billion valuation for the New York-based company, which was founded in 2024. 5. (tied) Vinci , $250M, AI for engineering: Vinci, developer of an AI computational platform for hardware engineers to design products, closed on $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. Advent , Temasek and Xora led the round for the Palo Alto, California-based company. 5. (tied) Atomic Machines , $250M, micro-manufacturing: Emeryville, California-based Atomic Machines, a startup working on AI-native digital manufacturing systems to build micro-machines directly from code, emerged from stealth and said it has raised $250 million to date from a long list of investors. 7. Voltus , $225M, energy distribution: Voltus, provider of a distributed energy platform aimed at bolstering grid flexibility, picked up $225 million in Series D funding. Generation Investment Management , Activate Capital and Vitol led the financing for the San Francisco-based startup. 8. (tied) Type One Energy , $200M, fusion: Knoxville, Tennessee-based Type One Energy, a developer of fusion energy technology, secured $200 million in Series B financing led by Breakthrough Energy Ventures and Clutterbuck Capital . 8. (tied) Ledgebrook , $200M, insurance: Ledgebrook, an AI-powered specialty insurance platform, closed on $200 million in equity financing co-led by Allianz X and Rockefeller Capital Management . The round brings total funding to date for Boston-based Ledgebrook to around $315 million, per Crunchbase data . 8. (tied) Arena , $200M, AI evaluation: Arena, provider of a platform for evaluating AI models, pulled in $200 million in Series B funding and said it has exceeded a $100 million annual revenue run rate. Lightspeed Venture Partners and Khosla Ventures led the round, which set a $3.1 billion valuation for the company. Methodology We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Oct. 3-9, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week. ]]> https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/Top_10_.jpeg Active Investors Kept Up The Deal Pace In Q3, Even As Funding Fell https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/q3-2026-active-investors-kept-deal-pace-a16z-insight-sequoia/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 11:00:56 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94203 Active startup investors largely kept up or increased their dealmaking pace in the third quarter, even as overall venture funding declined with the absence of new record megarounds for AI leaders. newContent: We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs.rss We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more en-US 60 RETR: Customer Success Manager Anywhere in the World 🇺🇸 United States of America Virginia Sales and Marketing Full-Time <img src="https://we-work-remotely.imgix.net/logos/0171/5755/logo.gif?ixlib=rails-4.0.0&w=50&h=50&dpr=2&fit=fill&auto=compress" /> <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> Remote <br /><strong>URL:</strong> <a href="https://retr.app/">https://retr.app/</a> </p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>About RETR</span></strong></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>RETR is a mortgage market intelligence platform. Loan officers use us to find the real estate agents worth building relationships with, mortgage companies use us to recruit top producers, and lenders use us to decide who to lend their money through. More than 55% of the Top 100 mortgage lenders are customers.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>We were founded in 2022, we are bootstrapped and profitable, and we have never taken outside money. We grew because loan officers told other loan officers about us. That word of mouth is the whole company in one sentence, and it is why customer outcomes are not a service function here. They are the growth engine.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>We are fully remote and we operate on a few principles: </span>lead with value, do the right thing, be generous without keeping score<span>. We hire for honesty, integrity, fairness, accountability, and excellence, and we have very little appetite for process that does not earn its place.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>The role</span></strong></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>This is one of the first Customer Success Managers at RETR, and you will own a book of our enterprise customers end to end: the relationships, the value they get, the renewal, and the growth.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>Our enterprise customers are held today by the founders, sales, support, and enablement, and they are held well. </span>This role exists because the book has outgrown what any of them can carry alongside their own jobs. You get a defined set of accounts and the time to go deep on them: exactly how each one is doing, what it needs next, and where it should be a year from now.</p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>You will report to our VP of Customer Advocacy and work alongside the account executives who own new business and large expansions, and the trainers who run onboarding and group sessions.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>What you own</span></strong></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>Four things. Everything else you do should move one of them.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>A plan for every customer.</span></strong><span> A short written plan for every account in your book: why they bought, who the people are, what they are trying to accomplish, how they actually use the product, where the risk is, and what happens next. New accounts get one within 30 days. Plans get refreshed before every review and every renewal.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>The renewal.</span></strong><span> You own the path to renewal from the day the account joins your book, not from 30 days out. Risk gets named early, in writing, with a plan against it. Nothing should churn without someone having seen it coming.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>Expansion.</span></strong><span> Growth comes from value: </span>new use cases, new features, new product lines, new teams and branches, and the seats that follow once people see what it is worth.<span> You run the smaller expansions yourself and bring in an account executive on the larger ones. Part of your pay is tied to this, and it should feel like the natural result of doing the rest of the job well.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>Advocates.</span></strong><span> Healthy customers become references, case studies, testimonials, referrals, and beta participants. In an industry this relationship-driven, a customer willing to vouch for us is worth more than most marketing we could buy.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>Underneath those four, the work is: knowing how customers use RETR and helping them use it better, building relationships with executive sponsors and daily users alike, reading health from adoption and conversation rather than guessing, and bringing what you hear back into the company so the product and the experience get better.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>What this role is not</span></strong></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>It is not reactive account management, and it is not a job you win by holding a set number of calls a week. Calls matter, but what matters is what happens on them: the relationship built, the plan moved, the value shown, the joy created.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>It is not a support queue. We have a support team and they are good. You are not the escalation path for every ticket in your book.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>Because we are still building the Customer Advocacy function, you won't be stepping into a perfectly defined playbook. You'll help create it. We want someone who is energized by that.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>How we work</span></strong></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>RETR is intentionally lean. Automation before hiring, systems before managers, one to many before one to one. Technology and AI should absorb the work that does not need human judgment, so our people spend their time where people are worth the most: understanding a customer's business, solving a real problem, building a relationship, finding the opportunity nobody else saw.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>So we do not want CSMs living in spreadsheets or doing repetitive admin. We want them thinking, and immersed/obsessed with our customers.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>We are fully remote and async first. We write things down. We measure what you deliver, and in this role that is the health of your book.</span></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><strong><span>What success looks like</span></strong></p> <p class="MsoNormal"><span>A great CSM here can answer these about any account, at any moment, without opening a file:</span></p> <ul> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>Why did this customer buy RETR?</span></li> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>How are they using it today, and who actually uses it?</span></li> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>Are they getting value, and how do we know?</span></li> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>Who inside the organization cares, and who signs the renewal?</span></li> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>Where could we create more value for them?</span></li> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>What could cost us this renewal?</span></li> <li class="MsoNormal"><span>What happens next, and when?</span></li> &l
